title: Thirty spokes
hookLine: thirty spokes share a hub, but the empty center makes the wheel useful (Tao Te Ching 11)

lines: FILL IT, AND THE CART STOPS.
cards: An old wooden cart wheel. Spokes run out from the middle like the lines of a sun in a child's drawing, and they all meet in a thick block at the center called the hub. Look closer at the hub.
There's a hole through it, where the axle goes. Fill it in with solid wood, make the hub perfect and complete, and the cart goes nowhere.
Chapter eleven of the Tao Te Ching starts right there, at the hole in the middle of the wheel.

teach.h: THE HOLE IN THE HUB TURNS THE WHEEL.
teach.b: First, the wheel. In James Legge's translation, the chapter opens: "The thirty spokes unite in the one nave; but it is on the empty space (for the axle), that the use of the wheel depends."
Nave is an old English word for the hub. The spokes are the part you'd photograph. The empty space is the part that turns.

teach.h: A POT'S HOLLOW, A ROOM'S OPENINGS.
teach.b: A pot is shaped from clay, but you use the hollow inside it. A room is made by cutting doors and windows into walls, and you live in the openings and the space they enclose. Each works because of what isn't there.

teach.h: WHAT'S THERE, AND WHAT ISN'T, AS A PAIR.
teach.b: What is there gives a thing its benefit, the last line says; what isn't there makes it useful. It doesn't say the solid parts don't matter. A wheel with no spokes is just a hole.
The wood and the empty space work as a pair. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. A calendar is a kind of wheel.

The meetings are the spokes, and they're what people notice. But a day packed solid has no hub left for anything to turn in: no room to think, no gap for someone to call, no pause between one thing and the next.

teach.h: AN OPEN HOUR IN A FULL DAY.
teach.b: Read this way, the open hour isn't wasted space.
It may be the part that lets the rest of the day move.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter eleven as a reason to value empty space, in a room, a schedule or a conversation, rather than filling every gap.

games.q: you're building a wheel and want the hub as strong as it can be. what do you do with the hole in the middle?
o: leave it empty, for the axle.
games.why: the chapter says the use of the wheel depends on the empty space. fill the hole and the cart goes nowhere.

practice: Look around for an empty space that's doing a job: the inside of a mug, the gap under a door, the floor where people walk. Rest your eyes on it and notice what it makes possible.
Then sit in the space this pause makes, with nothing to fill it.
